---
title: "Concepts"
---

tether borrows [jj](https://jj-vcs.dev)'s working-copy and operation-log
ideas -- `new REV` to start on top of a commit, the stale-working-copy check,
an op log with `undo` -- and applies them to the state of external systems
that keep their own history. It is not jj for data: the section after the
table says where the two part ways.

## The working copy is the manifests

A dataset is a directory holding `tether.toml` and `.tether/objects/<key>.toml`,
one manifest per registered object. A manifest names the object (`kind` +
`locator`), its policy, and -- once committed -- its recorded `state` and, if
any, its `pin`. Committing a dataset means committing those manifests to the
enclosing git/jj repository. History, branching, bookmarks, workspaces, and
sharing are therefore the VCS's, not tether's. What the VCS cannot see -- what
tether did to the *stores* to get there -- goes in tether's own
[operation log](#the-operation-log).

### jj vocabulary, where it maps

| jj | tether |
| --- | --- |
| working copy | the VCS working dir; the committed thing is the manifests |
| snapshot on every command | **snapshot**: concurrent fan-out fingerprint -- of every object on `verify`, `status --snapshot`, `tether snapshot`; of the objects this checkout can have moved on `commit`. A plain `status` shows the last one with its age |
| `jj commit` | **pin** the working branches' heads + write state into manifests + `jj/git commit`; untouched objects keep their pin |
| `jj new <rev>` | checkout + **fork** decision per object: a writable branch created on the first write (`--eager`: now), or kept if it already sits at the pin |
| stale working copy | per object: the committed state a fork was taken from is recorded; a manifest that now says otherwise refuses writes to that object until `new` |
| `jj diff` | **diff**: object-level manifest diff; `--content` asks each backend for its native diff |
| `jj log` | **log**: an object's *native* history (snapshots / versions / commits); ids feed `add --at` |
| untouched file stays as committed | an object with no working branch keeps its **pin** from commit to commit; `commit` does not contact it |
| `jj git fetch` + rebase | **pull**: move such objects to their upstream branch head (`locator.branch`); held in the workspace until the next commit pins it. `commit --pull` / `[commit] pull` does it on every commit |
| detached head | an object registered `--at` a state: its *initial* position; the first commit pins it, `new` forks from it, `pull` moves it onto the branch |
| -- | **verify** (pins still resolve) and **gc** (drop unreferenced pins, dead workspaces' branches) |
| `jj squash --into main` | **promote**: move each system's base branch to the fork -- fast-forward if the base is unchanged since the fork point, native merge where one exists, refuse otherwise |
| `jj abandon` | **abandon**: the VCS drops the commits (later manifests kept as they were) and the `gc` plan for what that freed is shown or applied |
| `jj restore --from REV FILE` | **restore**: reset one object's working branch to what `REV` pinned; the manifests and the other branches stay |
| `jj workspace forget` | **forget-workspace**: the VCS forgets the checkout and that workspace's working branches are deleted (safety-checked) in one step |
| `jj squash` | the VCS's own; what history no longer names, `gc` releases |
| `jj op log` / `jj undo` | **ops** / **undo**: tether's own log of what each command did to the stores, and the reversal of an entry where the store still allows it; **repair** rebuilds what a manifest promises |
| -- | **export** / **publish** (history as SQL tables) and **import** (the object set from a registry query) |

### Where tether is not jj

- **`commit` does not imply `new`.** `jj commit` describes the change and
  starts a fresh one on top. `tether commit` pins your working branches' heads
  and records them; the branches stay, the next write lands on the same
  branch, and `new` afterwards reuses it. Only `new REV` moves you. A branch
  accumulates commits the way a git branch does, not the way a jj change does.
- **Snapshots are on demand.** Reading an object's state is a network
  round-trip, so `status` is local and `status --snapshot`, `verify`, and
  `commit` (for the objects this checkout can have moved) fan out.
- **The stores are remotes.** Pins are what commits reference; working
  branches are local branches; `pull` is fetch and rebase; `promote` is the
  push to `main`. `behind` and `pulled` make sense in that frame, not jj's.

## Commits hold pins; the working copy holds branches

Two things are versioned, in two places.

A **dataset commit** records, for every object, an exact *state* and -- where
the system can hold one -- a *pin*: a native ref that keeps that state alive.
Nothing about a commit points at anything that moves: not a branch, not
"latest", not a path's current contents. That is what makes
`tether open KEY --rev C` a reproducible read months later, and what `verify`
checks.

The **working copy** (`.tether/workspace.toml`, per checkout, untracked)
records where each object *is between commits* -- its position:

| Position | Held as | Fingerprinted by `commit`? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a working branch that exists | `[working_refs]` | yes: its head is what the next commit pins |
| a working branch decided by `new` but not yet created | `[pending_forks]` -- forked from the pin on the first writable `open` | no: until it exists, the object sits at the pin |
| the base branch itself (`write = "direct"`) | `[working_refs]` = the base branch | yes |
| a state taken by `pull` but not yet committed | `[pulled]` | no: the held state *is* the position |
| nothing (a committed object nobody here is writing to) | -- | no: it keeps its pin |
| not committed yet | -- | yes, once: the branch head or `--at` |

The rule falls out of the table: `commit` contacts an object only if this
checkout can have moved it; everything else keeps its pin, the way a file you
did not edit stays as the parent commit had it. The world moving on is not a
change to *your* position -- `status --snapshot` shows it as `behind`, and
`tether pull` takes it (fetch and rebase, for data; `[commit] pull = true` on
every commit).

`locator.branch` is the object's *upstream*: what the first commit pins,
`pull` reads, `promote` lands on, and `direct` writes to. `--at` is only where
a new object starts.

## State, pin, fork

For each object a backend implements three things, in increasing order of what
the system must support:

- **State**: what the object *is* right now -- an Icechunk `snapshot_id`, a
  Neon `(lsn, next_xid, branch)`, a Delta `version`, a file's sha256, a
  directory's digest over its files' sha256s.
  Comparing states is how drift is detected without watching anything.
- **Pin**: a durable, GC-proof native reference to a state, named
  `tether.<pin_id>` -- an Icechunk tag, a protected Neon child branch, a git
  tag, a Lance tag, a Dolt tag. `pin_id = <dataset-id>.<blake2b(kind, locator
  identity, content state)[:16]>`, so identical state on the same object yields
  the same pin within a dataset and re-committing an unchanged object is a
  no-op. The dataset id in front is the [namespace](#namespaces).
- **Fork**: a fresh writable branch created off a pin -- or, for objects with
  `pin = "record"`, straight off the recorded state, skipping the native ref
  entirely. `tether new` decides one per Forkable object, named
  `tether.ws.<dataset-id>.<workspace-id>.<key-slug>-<key-hash>`, so neither
  datasets, workspaces, nor look-alike keys collide, and by default
  creates it lazily on the first writable `open` (pins are durable, so the
  branch can wait; pin-less objects fork immediately because their recorded
  state cannot wait). `--eager` creates them all during `new`.

## Namespaces

`tether.toml` carries an 8-hex `[dataset] id`, generated by `init` and
committed, so every clone of the dataset shares it. Every native ref tether
creates starts with it: pins are `tether.<id>.<hash>`, working branches
`tether.ws.<id>.<workspace>.<key>`. `gc` only ever considers refs in its own
namespace -- several datasets can pin the same Icechunk repo or Neon project
and none of them can delete another's pins or branches, `--force-prune`
included; foreign refs are counted in the plan's notes and left alone. The
price is that the same content pinned by two datasets is two refs.

## Plans

Every command that writes to an external system (`commit` pins, `new` forks,
`gc` unpins and deletes branches, `promote`, `import`, `repair`) is a
read-only **plan** followed by an **apply**. `--dry-run` prints the plan,
`--plan FILE` saves it, `--from-plan FILE` applies it later; apply re-checks
that states and manifests still match what the plan recorded and refuses
otherwise (`StalePlanError`). The Python API exposes the same pairs:
`plan_commit`/`apply_commit`, `plan_new`/`apply_new`, `plan_gc`/`apply_gc`,
and so on.

## The operation log

The VCS records the manifests. It cannot see which native refs `commit`
created, which branches `new` forked or reset and what their heads were
before, what `gc` deleted, or where `promote` moved a base branch from. Every
apply therefore appends an entry to `.tether/ops.jsonl` -- per workspace,
untracked, append-only, like jj's own `op log` -- holding the plan it applied,
what it did, and what it replaced. `tether ops` lists it.

`tether undo [ID]` reverses an entry *where the store still allows it* and
says exactly what it could not reverse:

| Undoing a ... | does |
| --- | --- |
| `commit` | uncommits it (the manifests become working-tree changes again; the pins stay, still referenced) while it is still the working copy's parent |
| `new` / a lazy fork | deletes the branches it created, re-points the ones it reset to their recorded heads, restores `workspace.toml`, returns the VCS working copy if it has not moved since |
| `gc` | recreates deleted branches from their recorded heads and listings from the VCS; deleted **pins are irreversible** -- once a manifest references them again, `repair` recreates them while the state is still reachable |
| `import` / `add` / `remove` | restores the manifests |
| `promote` | is refused, with the previous base heads printed for a manual reset; backends only fast-forward |

`tether undo --to ID` walks back through every newer operation in turn -- the
per-operation-delta version of `jj op restore`, which stops where a store
will not follow. A branch that gained writes since the operation is never
deleted or reset silently: `undo` refuses until you commit them or pass
`--discard`. The same
rule applies to `new` itself -- a working branch holding writes you never
committed is only reset with `--discard`.

`tether repair` is the other direction: given the manifests, rebuild what they
promise. A pin whose native ref is gone is recreated from the recorded state
(as long as the store still has it); a working branch this workspace expects
but the store lost is forked again. `--all-history` checks every commit's pins.

What `jj undo` / `git reset` can and cannot do is unchanged by all this: they
revert the manifests, never the stores. Use them for the VCS side, `tether
undo` for tether's. When they remove a dataset commit behind tether's back,
`status` says so (`warning: dataset commit ... is no longer in VCS history`)
and `ops` flags the entry, with whether the pins that commit made are still
named by the working tree.

## Capability tiers

Backends declare capabilities; commands degrade explicitly by tier.

- **Observed** (`FINGERPRINT`): drift detection only. `commit` records the state
  and marks it `recoverable = false`. A local directory by content hash, an
  unversioned S3 prefix.
- **Addressable** (`+ ADDRESSABLE`): the recorded state can be read back later
  with nothing to create or GC. An S3 object in a versioned bucket, a Delta
  version, a DuckLake snapshot.
- **Pinnable** (`+ PIN`): a durable native ref can be created and deleted;
  `verify` and `gc` apply.
- **Forkable** (`+ FORK`): a writable branch can be created off a pin; `new`
  forks and `open` returns a writable handle. Icechunk, Neon, Iceberg, Lance,
  lakeFS, Dolt, git/jj.

Orthogonal flags refine behavior: `CHEAP_FINGERPRINT` (metadata only),
`RETENTION_BOUND` (recoverability expires with a retention window),
`NEEDS_QUIESCENCE` (commit checks for active writers), `ATOMIC_REF`
(create-if-absent pins), `DIFF` (native content diffs), `HISTORY` (native
log), `BRANCH_IS_STORAGE` (deleting a branch reclaims its data; `gc` never
prunes such a branch without force), `PROMOTE` (fast-forward the base branch
to a fork) and `MERGE` (three-way merge a fork into the base).

## Handles, not data

tether is never in the data path. `open` returns a typed handle carrying the
native address -- an Icechunk session on the right branch or tag, a Postgres
URL, a `DeltaTable` at a version, a `lakefs://repo/ref/prefix/` URI -- and steps
aside. You read and write with the system's own library.

## Stale working copies

jj's stale-working-copy check, applied to external branches. The workspace
remembers the committed state each working branch was forked from; if the
manifest now says otherwise, the branch no longer starts where the dataset
says it does and the object is *stale*: `status` names it, writable `open`
refuses with `StaleWorkingCopyError`, and `tether new` clears it.

- Stale: a teammate committed that object; you `jj new`'d to another revision.
- Never stale: your own commits; other objects being added or removed;
  `direct` objects (they write to the base branch).

## Content and address

A state's keys do two jobs:

- **Content** keys say what the data is: an Icechunk snapshot id, a Neon
  `next_xid`, a git sha. Equality (drift, `commit`'s unchanged check,
  `promote`), pin ids, and listing names use only these.
- **Address** keys say where to find or cut it and can move without the data
  changing: Neon's `lsn` advances on checkpoints; git's `change_id` exists only
  when jj is installed. Backends list them in `VOLATILE_KEYS`; `open`, `pin`,
  and `verify` get the whole state.

Iceberg's `metadata_location`, which changes on every table commit on any
branch, is in neither: it is not part of the state at all.

## Drift

`status --snapshot` (or a scheduled `tether snapshot`) catches drift without a
daemon. An Observed object registered as immutable (the default for `file`)
that changes on disk is an *error*; a system that moved past an object's pin
is `behind` (take it with `pull`); a working branch that moved is `modified`
and will be pinned on the next commit. `verify` answers the other question --
do the pins we recorded still resolve to the states we recorded? -- cheaply by
default, deeply with `--deep`, and across every commit with `--all-history`.

## Listings

A directory or prefix state is only a digest, so it cannot be diffed on its
own. At commit time the `file` backend hands tether a per-file listing, stored
content-addressed under `.tether/listings/` and committed with the manifests
(the same trick as DVC's `.dir` files). `diff --content` compares two listings
file by file; `gc` prunes listings no manifest references.

## jj or tether?

Both work on the same repository, so the question comes up constantly. The
rule: **an operation gets a tether command when it has two halves -- one in
the VCS, one in the stores -- that must happen together.** If it only touches
files and history, use jj or git directly; tether will notice what it needs
to (a moved working copy makes objects stale, a vanished dataset commit shows
in `status` and `ops`).

| You want to | Use | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| record the dataset's state | `tether commit` | pins every object in its store, *then* commits the manifests |
| start working on a revision | `tether new REV` | moves the working copy *and* decides a working branch per object |
| look at another revision without writing | `jj new REV` / `jj edit` / `git switch` | nothing to fork; tether reports the objects as stale until you `tether new` |
| reset one object to an older commit's state | `tether restore KEY --from REV` | the branch lives in a store |
| drop dataset commits | `tether abandon REV` | the VCS drops them, descendants keep their manifests as snapshots, and the pins that just freed up are planned for `gc` |
| edit history otherwise: describe, squash, rebase, split | jj / git | manifests are files; nothing in a store changes. Run `tether gc` afterwards if commits disappeared |
| merge two dataset branches | jj / git merge | conflicts are per manifest file; then `tether verify` and `tether new` |
| bookmarks, branches, push, fetch, review | jj / git | sharing is the VCS's |
| open a second checkout | `jj workspace add` / `git worktree add` | the first tether command there starts its own tether workspace |
| finish with a checkout | `tether forget-workspace` | the VCS forgets it *and* its working branches are deleted (safely) |
| undo tether's last operation | `tether undo` (`--to ID` for several) | the VCS cannot see what tether did to the stores |
| undo any other VCS operation | `jj undo` / the reflog | tether did nothing there; `status` warns if a dataset commit went with it |
| a store lost a pin or branch a manifest names | `tether repair` | manifests are the source of truth |
| reclaim storage | `tether gc` (after the VCS surgery above) | what history no longer names, the stores can release |

Two habits keep the halves aligned: `tether status` after any VCS operation
that moved the working copy or changed manifests, and `tether new` before
writing again.

## What tether does not do

- Sit in the data path. `open` hands back the system's native handle and
  steps aside.
- Run between commands. There is no daemon or watcher; every state is
  compared when a command asks.
- Cross-system atomicity. A commit records each object's state within a
  capture window; point-consistency requires quiesced writers.
- Reimplement history, branching, or sharing. That is the VCS's job. tether's
  own `ops` / `undo` / `repair` cover only what tether did to the stores --
  the part the VCS cannot see.
- Queries or transactions across systems.
